fix(bot): a claim's days count from a new assignment, and the periods are 10 and 14 days (#405)

The contributor bot counts a claim's days from a new assignment, and
waits 14 days before it releases a claim.

Closes #401

This changes `scripts/bot/atlas_bot.py`, a script that a workflow runs
with a credential that can write. What changes in what it does is listed
below. **The bot runs from `main`, so this pull request changes nothing
for a claim until it is there.** The daily job stays paused until then.

## What was wrong

Seen on #253: claimed on 2026-09-29; the draft pull request #272 into
`dev`, with `Closes #253`, was opened 13 hours later; the bot reminded
on 10-04 and released the claim on 10-06; the owner assigned the
contributor again by hand; the bot released the claim again on 10-07.

Two causes, both established from the code:

1. **On `main` the bot asks only GitHub's own link** between an issue
and a pull request. GitHub makes that link only for a pull request into
the default branch. Every contribution here goes into `dev`, so the bot
on `main` sees no claim as having a pull request.
- `dev` has had the fix for this since 2026-09-28: an open pull request
of the claimant, into any branch, that names the issue keeps the claim.
That change never reached `main`.
2. **The days counted from the first `/claim` comment.** A new
assignment by a maintainer did not start them again, so the claim was
released on the next daily run. This is on `dev` too, and it is what
this pull request fixes.

Shown on the live board with the bot's own dry-run mode, which prints
what it would write and writes nothing (2026-10-07, 17:26Z):

| The bot of | What it would do today |
|---|---|
| `main` | Release #253 again: take the contributor off, set the card to
Ready, post "this claim is released: no linked pull request after 7
days" |
| this pull request | Nothing |

## What changes

- **The count starts again with a new assignment.** The days run from
the newest of the `/claim` comment and the last time that person was
assigned to the issue, by the bot or by hand. The bot reads this from
the issue's events. An assignment older than the claim changes nothing.
A reminder from before the new assignment does not count as sent.
- **The periods:** a reminder after **10** days without a pull request
(5 before), release after **14** (7 before). They are in
`.github/atlas-bot.yml`. CONTRIBUTING states them, and now also says "as
a draft if it is not ready" and `Refs #<issue>` for an issue that must
stay open. A new test keeps the two numbers in CONTRIBUTING the same as
the settings.
- **One more read for the bot:** the events of an issue, and only for a
claim that is at least 10 days old and has no pull request. No new
write.

## What does not change

- The rule which pull request keeps a claim: an open one, by the
claimant, into any branch, that names the issue in its title or text.
`Closes #N` and `Refs #N` do, and so does any other naming of `#N`. A
pull request by another person does not, and a closed one does not.
- This is wider than "only `Closes`, `Fixes`, `Resolves` or `Refs`". A
narrower rule would release a claim whose pull request says "Part of
#N", which is the fault of #253 in another form. A wider rule only keeps
a claim a little longer, and a maintainer can end it.
- `sync` and `/claim` do not use the link lookup. Only the daily run
does.
- GOVERNANCE and the translated pages do not state these two periods, so
they are not changed. ("7 days" in GOVERNANCE is the comment period of
an RFC.)

## Proof

- `tests/infrastructure/test_atlas_bot.py`: 79 tests (63 before). Among
them:
- the case of #253: a claim, a draft pull request into `dev` with
`Closes` 13 hours later, the daily run 15 days after the claim: no
reminder, no release;
- `Refs`, `Fixes` and `Resolves` keep a claim; a pull request by another
person does not; a closed pull request does not;
- a hand assignment 3 or 9 days ago: nothing; 10 or 13 days ago: a new
reminder; 14 days ago: release;
- the real API class, with the network replaced: only open pull requests
are asked for; the newest assignment of that person is read from the
events, and a removal is not an assignment.
- The shape of the events was checked against #253's own (five assigned
and unassigned events, each with the person and the time).
- 13 planted changes and 2 controls, each tried alone against the tests,
in a Linux container with a memory limit and a time limit of 90 s for
each run. The controls stay green; each planted change turns at least
one test red. Among them: a hand assignment does not start the count
again; an assignment older than the claim moves the count back; an old
reminder counts as sent; a pull request of another person keeps the
claim; closed pull requests are asked for too; the assignment of another
person counts; a removal counts as an assignment; the old periods come
back; CONTRIBUTING states another number than the settings.
- One planted change stayed green at first (a removal counts as an
assignment). The test of the events now has a removal that is newer than
the last assignment.
- `tests/infrastructure` and `tests/contracts`: 816 passed, 30 skipped.
ruff, the size check, the minimum-Python check and the YAML check pass.

## Known limits

- A claim whose pull request was closed or merged while the issue stays
open is counted again from the claim or the last assignment. A
maintainer who wants to keep it assigns the person again.
- The count restarts for every new assignment of that person, also one
that the person makes themself where GitHub lets them.
